Licence
lī´sĕns
n. (leave or permission formally granted)
From the Latin licentia, leave, from licet, it is permitted. Both occurrences are in Acts, and both concern a Roman officer granting a prisoner the right to speak.

Biblical Definition

Paul, seized in the temple and taken into custody, asks the chief captain for leave to address the crowd: “And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue” (Acts 21:40). The second use states the Roman legal principle that kept Paul alive through the rest of the book: “To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him” (Acts 25:16). Festus is explaining to Agrippa why he would not hand Paul over to the Sanhedrin. The apostle's own account of the same protection is his appeal: “I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest” (Acts 25:10). Providence used a pagan procedural rule to carry the gospel to Rome, and Paul says as much of his imprisonment: “But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Philippians 1:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines licence as leave; permission; authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.

expand to see more

LICENSE, n. Leave; permission; authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.

LICENSE, n. Excess of liberty; exorbitant freedom; freedom abused, or used in contempt of law or decorum.

MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.

ACCUSER, n. One who accuses or blames; an officer who prefers a charge against a person.

APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior tribunal.

Key Scripture

Acts 21:40 — "And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,"

Acts 25:16 — "To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face , and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him."

Acts 25:10 — "Then said Paul, I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest."

Philippians 1:12 — "But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;"

Modern Corruption

The word has drifted from permission formally granted to liberty without restraint, and the modern sense is read back into a Bible that never uses it that way.

expand to see more

Webster already recorded both senses in 1828: licence as leave granted, and licence as liberty abused. English has since let the second sense swallow the first, so that a modern reader meets licence and hears permissiveness. Scripture uses only the first. In Acts the word describes a Roman officer granting a prisoner the right to speak — an act of lawful authority, carefully bounded, which the prisoner then uses. The distinction matters because the two senses are moral opposites: one is liberty under authority, the other liberty against it.

The theological application is the one Peter makes when he warns against using liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, and Jude when he describes men turning the grace of God into lasciviousness. Christian freedom in the Reformed confessions is always freedom granted — freedom from the curse of the law, from the dominion of sin, from the tyranny of men's consciences — and never freedom from the moral law as a rule of life. A believer who reasons from grace to permission has taken the word in the wrong sense, and Acts shows him the right one: leave given by a rightful authority, for a purpose, and answerable to the one who gave it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epitrepo (G2010), to permit or give leave; topos apologias, place of defence; apologeomai (G626), to answer for oneself; parresia (G3954), boldness of speech.

expand to see more

Greek epitrepo (G2010) — to turn over to, permit; Acts 21:40, when he had given him licence.

Greek apologia (G627) — a defence, verbal answer; the right Festus describes.

Greek apologeomai (G626) — to answer for oneself concerning a charge.

Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; how Paul used the leave granted.

Greek prokope (G4297) — furtherance, advance; Philippians 1:12, the gospel advanced by the arrest.

Usage

"“When he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs” — leave to address the crowd."

"“Have licence to answer for himself” — the Roman rule Festus cites."

"“Unto the furtherance of the gospel” — what providence made of the custody."
